To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cross price effect is the key to understanding entry prevention in a duopoly with fixed cost.

(a) the established firm may prevent entry, but this is not a prior condition; (b) the threat of predatory output increases after entry may make entry easier; and (c) the established firm's absolute advantage in demand and its cross-price effect have opposite effects on entry.
(i) an absolute advantage for an established firm may make it more difficult for the entrant to enter the market and (ii) a lower cross price elasticity of demand may make entry easier.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a model of duopolistic competition in which the established firm has a cost advantage over the potential entrant.
the conditions under which a duopolist may prevent entry and the conditions which make it more likely that entry will occur.
the conditions for the existence of entry barriers and the role of product differentiation in the process of entry and exit.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is not very useful.
entry barriers are not necessarily a priori constraints on competition, but may be a consequence of the interaction of market forces.
the model is not very useful for the analysis of entry barriers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the established firm can prevent the entry of a new firm by raising fixed costs and by increasing its excess capacity.

the model suggests that the threat of a large output increase after entry, which can be credible by carrying excess capacities prior to entry, may be a more effective way for preventing entry than a high fixed cost.
the threat of predatory pricing is a credible one, if the established firm can carry excess capacity prior to the entry of a potential competitor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
entry prevention can be a result of the established firm's market power and the threat of predatory pricing, and not a prior constraint.
entry barriers are not a necessary condition for leadership.
entry prevention is not the only barrier to entry.
